study_identification_part.si4_title: Individualized gray matter morphological abnormalities unveil two neuroanatomical obsessive-compulsive disorder subtypes

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To identify distinct OCD subtypes based on individualized gray matter morphological abnormalities compared to normative expectations, and to examine disease epicenters and molecular underpinnings of structural abnormalities in the identified subtypes.

rci7_preprocessing_pipeline.reason: The imaging data processing section provides detailed information about the preprocessing pipeline using CAT12 toolbox with specific processing steps.
rci7_preprocessing_pipeline.supporting_text: Voxel-wise gray matter volume (GMV) for each participant was derived using voxel-based morphometry in the CAT 12 toolbox (http://dbm.neuro.uni-jena.de/cat12/). The standard CAT 12 pipeline was followed, as detailed in reference [35]. This pipeline encompassed bias field correction, brain segmentation into gray and white matter and cerebrospinal fluid, correction for partial volume effects, normalization to Montreal Neurological Institute space, resampling to 1.5 mm³, and nonlinear modulation [35, 36]. Subsequently, the gray matter maps underwent smoothing with a 6-mm full width at half maximum Gaussian kernel.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Two-sample t-tests with FDR correction (p<0.05) to compare gray matter morphological abnormalities between each subtype and healthy controls, adjusting for sex, age, and TIV as covariates. Structural covariance network analysis using Pearson correlation to examine associations between regional abnormalities and SC-informed abnormalities (with permutation testing, 10,000 times). Disease epicenter mapping using permutation testing (10,000 times, p<0.01) to identify regions with highest atrophy likelihood based on regional abnormalities and SC-informed rankings. Multilinear regression models linking neurotransmitter receptor/transporter profiles to gray matter abnormalities for each subtype, with permutation testing (10,000 times) and FDR correction. Dominance analysis to assess relative importance of each neurotransmitter predictor across all subset models.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Two distinct OCD subtypes were identified with opposite patterns of gray matter morphological abnormalities (subtype 1 with increased GMV, subtype 2 with decreased GMV) relative to healthy controls, exhibiting divergent disease epicenters (subtype 1 in middle frontal gyrus; subtype 2 in striatum/thalamus/hippocampus) and distinct associations with neurotransmitter receptors (subtype 1 linked to 5HT1A; subtype 2 linked to 5HT2A).
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: Using individualized gray matter morphological abnormalities assessed via normative modeling, the study identified two robust OCD subtypes (N=49 and N=51) exhibiting contrasting patterns relative to healthy controls. Subtype 1 demonstrated significantly increased GMV in frontal gyrus, precuneus, insula, hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, amygdala, and temporal gyrus (FDR p<0.05), while subtype 2 showed significantly decreased GMV in frontal gyrus, precuneus, insula, superior parietal gyrus, temporal gyrus, and fusiform (FDR p<0.05). When all patients were combined, no significant GMV differences emerged compared to HCs. Structural covariance network analysis revealed significant correlations between regional abnormalities and SC-informed abnormalities for both subtypes (subtype 1: r=0.44, permutation pFDR<0.001; subtype 2: r=0.50, permutation pFDR<0.001). Disease epicenter analysis identified divergent epicenters: subtype 1 in middle frontal gyrus (permutation p<0.01) and subtype 2 in striatum, thalamus, and hippocampus (permutation p<0.01). Multilinear models linking neurotransmitter receptor/transporter profiles to GMV abnormalities showed good fit (adjusted R²=0.43 for subtype 1, R²=0.34 for subtype 2; all FDR-corrected permutation p<0.001). Dominance analysis revealed 5HT1A as the key receptor for subtype 1 and 5HT2A for subtype 2. Clinically, subtypes differed significantly in sex distribution (subtype 1: 73.5% male; subtype 2: 33.3% male; χ²=16.161, p<0.001) but not in age of onset, illness duration, or symptom severity (Y-BOCS). Sensitivity analyses confirmed high reproducibility (ARI=0.98±0.04 for subsample validation; ARI=0.74 across different brain atlases; ARI=0.62 for different distance metrics).

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Cross-sectional design limiting assessment of subtype stability/generalizability; limited clinical information restricting exploration of subtype differences in other clinical aspects; neurotransmitter associations based on publicly available datasets rather than individual measurements; lower educational level in OCD patients compared to controls (though no difference between subtypes); lack of external validation in independent datasets
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: First, it was conducted using a cross-sectional sample, raising questions about the stability and generalizability of the identified subtypes. Future studies should validate our results with independent and longitudinal datasets to confirm their robustness. Second, the limited clinical information available restricted our ability to explore potential differences in other clinical aspects between the subtypes. ... Third, individual variations in neurotransmitter systems may affect the observed associations between structural abnormalities and neurotransmitter systems, which were based on publicly available datasets [103]. Finally, patients with OCD in our study had lower educational levels compared to healthy controls.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: Study employed k-means clustering on individualized Z-score vectors (246×1) with optimal number of subtypes (k=2) determined by silhouette values. Reproducibility was extensively validated through: (1) random subsample analysis (90% of patients, 1000 iterations, ARI=0.98±0.04); (2) alternative brain atlas validation (AAL with 90 regions, ARI=0.74); (3) alternative distance metric validation (correlation distance instead of Euclidean, ARI=0.62). Disease epicenter mapping integrated structural covariance network information with regional abnormalities using a novel ranking approach combining regional atrophy and SC-informed abnormalities. Neurotransmitter analysis utilized publicly available PET-derived receptor/transporter atlas from Hansen et al., including 19 different receptor/transporter types across multiple neurotransmitter systems. Dominance analysis provided quantitative assessment of relative importance of each neurotransmitter predictor by evaluating all 2^n-1 possible subset models.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This is a single-site study conducted at First Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University with all participants of Han Chinese ethnicity. All OCD patients were first-episode and untreated at time of scanning. The normative model utilized the Brain Connectome Atlas (246 regions), with sensitivity analyses conducted using AAL atlas (90 regions). For disease epicenter analysis, a separate independent structural covariance network was constructed from another single-site dataset (Southwest University adult lifespan dataset, N=492, age 19-80 years). The study represents one of the first applications of normative modeling to identify neuroanatomical subtypes in OCD. Y-BOCS scores: OCD total mean 21.92±7.09; Subtype 1 mean 20.51±7.72; Subtype 2 mean 23.27±6.21 (no significant difference, p=0.051). Illness duration: OCD total mean 48.08±57.61 months; Subtype 1 mean 35.35±43.18 months; Subtype 2 mean 48.84±65.72 months (no significant difference, p=0.230). Age of onset: OCD total mean 16.45±10.13 years; Subtype 1 mean 17.40±9.34 years; Subtype 2 mean 15.54±10.86 years (no significant difference, p=0.360).
